items.title: David Silver and Lasse Espeholt of Ineffable Intelligence: A Superlearner for the Age of Experience

Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:32
Collectively, you know, we started with this kind of gray mush in our head. Thank you.

So I suppose I always had this conviction starting my PhD and going into the game of Go that the right approach to solve AI was through learning from experience, through systems that discovered things for themselves, that were learning through reinforcement learning to get better and better and better, and that that would be the thing which would lead to the emergence of intelligence and ultimately superintelligence. And so I suppose we were able to show that in the game of Go, but it's a conviction that has held true throughout my career, and here we are now applying that conviction, ineffable, trying to show that indeed superintelligence can emerge all the way through systems that learn from experience.

Speaker 1 | 02:48 - 03:39
And in terms of things which are different, although we are not pursuing the human data path that the LLM world has pursued, I do think there's lots of interesting lessons to learn from that. In particular, it was definitely a surprise to me how a system that was trained on a massive amount of data could then be very quickly fine tuned on a very small amount of data to completely change its behavior. That was something which I think was something which changed my mindset in terms of just suggesting that if you get things at the right scale, that a lot of things which seem incredibly hard or they might be very slow, that once you've kind of experienced enough data, that after that, the things that were slow can become very fast. I think that's a lesson that wasn't obvious to me in advance until it happened.

Speaker 2 | 03:39 - 03:56
Okay, we're going to come back to that later. You could have run this program inside DeepMind where could have probably had more access to compute than just about anybody. You decided the right thing to do was to start a new lab. Why'd you do that?

So I think that kind of realization also meant that this was something which just means that it's the best way to have impact upon the field through this approach.

That's right. Yeah, it's right.

Speaker 3 | 08:42 - 08:45

Speaker 1 | 08:45 - 09:29
It should be said as well. We worked together on some of the early approaches to combining reinforcement learning with deep learning and trying to scale things up. You know, the real science of doing right.

Speaker 2 | 52:54 - 53:01
So accelerate in simulation so we can understand what's happening and, you know, science around it and then careful in the real world.

Speaker 1 | 53:01 - 53:04
Yeah, I think that would be my summary. Yeah.

Speaker 2 | 53:04 - 53:29
I'd love to transition to talking a little bit about compute. This is going to be an incredibly compute expensive journey, and you are pushing the limits of what compute can do. I think both Google and NVIDIA have been great partners for you. Can you talk a little bit about your cluster? You're not simply renting spot compute from Neo Clouds like many other NeoLabs.

Speaker 2 | 53:29 - 53:37
You're actually some really serious work on your cluster and the different other forms of compute that you have. Can you just talk about your compute setup?

Speaker 3 | 53:37 - 54:17
Right, so, yeah, as I mentioned earlier, we are very fortunate with the compute that we have. We are the first customers of the largest real group and cluster on GCP by the end of the year. Well, actually started like one month from now. So we are extremely fortunate in that, and I actually feel quite bad about the startups that are getting compute now because it's becoming harder and harder. But yeah, so we have this, we have a grouping cluster, which is based on GPUs, like NVIDIA GPUs, which is really fortunate for us because it means that we can easily do simulation and training and inference.

Speaker 3 | 54:17 - 54:44
They are quite general chips. So that's amazing. Think the Vera Rubin specifically, they have this architecture where one rack can basically be considered one machine. There's a very high bandwidth between the nodes and one rack, which is very important for reinforcement learning where you have really fast iteration cycles compared to LLMs that are relatively speaking quite slow. So that's quite fortunate for us.

Speaker 3 | 54:44 - 55:18
And I think some of the things we did eight, ten years ago at Google, where we basically had abundant CPUs at Google that doesn't scale anymore. So we really need to make sure that everything we do is on the GPUs and we don't need millions of CPUs beyond these GPUs. So our simulations can run on the GPU inference and training and so on. So we have some good architectures for that. I think like the LLM companies now have kind of like the problems that we had many years ago where the need like sandboxes running on CPUs, like simulating computers and so on.

Speaker 3 | 55:18 - 55:21
And we're trying to not put ourselves in that situation.

Speaker 2 | 55:23 - 55:38
All the compute, is it roughly fungible between the different things that you're doing? I imagine you're building crucibles and then you're kind of doing these big rollouts where the agents are actually learning. Is that the rough buckets of what compute is being used for?

Speaker 3 | 55:38 - 55:44
Yeah, you could split it up into training inference and simulation.

Speaker 2 | 55:45 - 55:51
Is the same compute equally good at training inference and simulation? Okay.

Speaker 3 | 55:51 - 56:26
So I think it's pretty clear what has happened with GPUs over the last many years, or like since deep learning took off, is that they've been more and more tailored towards training, and maybe in the last few years also inference, but less about simulation. Right? We are, like similarly to the LLM companies, we also want to be in the case where scaling loss matters. We know that roughly if you add this amount of compute and experiences, then we get a certain amount of quality out of that.

Speaker 2 | 56:26 - 56:32
So I guess if GPUs aren't great for scaling simulation, then what's the solution?

Speaker 3 | 56:32 - 56:49
Right, so there are many different solutions here, right? So there's like model based reinforcement learning, where the model becomes much more expensive compared to the simulation. So there's many different tricks you can do. There's various approaches for replay buffers or reusing data many times. So yeah, there are ways around that.

Speaker 3 | 56:50 - 57:00
And other than that, we do spend quite some effort on just making the simulations as fast as possible and make the best use of the GPUs. Are

Speaker 2 | 57:01 - 57:04
you seeing scaling laws yet or is it too early to say?

Speaker 3 | 57:05 - 57:34
So for reinforcement learning, scaling laws are slightly different. Scaling laws is the component of how much compute you put in, how much data you put in, and the model size. Reinforcement learning is a little bit different because the problem is non stationary. So as you progress in the problem, the data changes, the data distribution changes. So they are a little bit different, it's a very interesting research direction.

Speaker 2 | 57:34 - 57:42
I understand they're different, but are you seeing some sort of scaling law where more compute in gets you closer to achieving the goals, or is it hard to say right now?

Speaker 3 | 57:42 - 57:53
Yeah, but it's something we are actively pushing towards. And especially as we are transitioning from a smaller cluster to the bigger cluster, we want to be ready for that.

Speaker 2 | 57:54 - 58:15
Leise, at the beginning, when David introduced you, he mentioned that you had done some very foundational work to compute and algorithms for reinforcement learning upon which the field really relies on today. Maybe talk about some of that work and in particular your work around Impala and Seed. What are those and how do they relate to the work that you're doing at ineffable?

Speaker 3 | 58:16 - 58:56
So when I joined the deep learning team at DeepMind, most people were running single machine, CPU based reinforcement learning. So the scale was quite small. So what I did together with colleagues was to make an agent, reinforcement learning agent that really utilized GPUs that could scale linear with compute. I think partially because it was very efficient, it was very good at scaling. And the third thing was it very easy to extend and modify and do whatever you wanted with it, contributed to it being the most popular reinforcement agent at the company.

Speaker 3 | 58:56 - 59:25
And I think at one point, most RL team used it or derivatives of it. So that was quite successful and quite a nice project to work on. Then later on, we got TBUs. We got racks of these TBUs, so we need to scale beyond that. So some of my work at Google Brain, after I left DeepMind to found the Google Brain Amsterdam office, was to scale to racks of TBUs, and that produce called SeedRL.

Speaker 3 | 59:26 - 59:43
So that was really about utilizing the TBUs both for inference and training in the best possible way while keeping the environments as flexible as you want it to. It could be anything from Go to very expensive physics simulations.

Speaker 2 | 59:43 - 59:46
And how's that being used at ineffable?

Speaker 3 | 59:46 - 1:00:11
Yeah, so, well, we actually implemented a few of those algorithms, also like derivatives of these algorithms. So that is like what we are using today. Depending on the environments, we use different algorithms, there are pros and cons between them. So yeah, we talked about we have some very simple, fast to simulate environments and also some that are more expensive.

Speaker 1 | 1:00:12 - 1:00:33
So for those who are working on large scale RL architectures today and haven't read those original papers, it's definitely worth a look because I think you'll discover that many of the ideas that are currently in use trace back to those early work that Lasser did and figured out, which was a little bit prescient,

Speaker 3 | 1:00:33 - 1:01:02
I would say. I think it's actually kind of fun to see the reinforcement learning space now versus like ten years ago, or let's say like eight years ago maybe. The LLM community is also using reinforcement learning, in particular the last two years. And a lot of the things that they're using are being rediscovered, approaches that we used many years ago. So it's kind of interesting to see, with a lot of novelty as well on top of it.

Speaker 2 | 1:01:03 - 1:01:06
Can you talk a little bit about your team? How big is the team right now?

Speaker 1 | 1:01:06 - 1:01:34
We have intentionally kept the team relatively small. So we're not in a hurry to build a giant organization. I think you can do an awful lot nowadays with a small number of incredibly talented people. So we have hired 20 people in total. And yeah, the people we've hired, it's about finding some of the exceptionally talented people.

Speaker 1 | 1:01:34 - 1:01:58
But it's not just about talent for us. It's also about bringing together people who are kind, collaborative human beings. That's really important to the kind of culture we're trying to build. And people who are really well aligned with the kind of mission that we're following, and people that sort of fit the needs that we have. So we try and build the team with the right set of skills as well.

Speaker 1 | 1:01:59 - 1:02:13
So all of those four things are really important. And we kind of have very high standards and very high expectations of the people that come in. So we'll be very lucky to get some amazing, really amazing people.

Speaker 3 | 1:02:13 - 1:02:37
And so just to tie it to the compute as well, This relatively small amount of people so far means that we have a lot of compute per person. And these days you can do a lot of experiments just like one person. So it's really also to keep the compute to person ratio quite high. So we're not fighting for resources from day one. I

Speaker 2 | 1:02:37 - 1:02:59
think three of the co founders worked together on AlphaStar. Many of you did work together. Are you assembling the Avengers, especially given the recent changes from DeepMind, are you assembling the Avengers of folks that you've worked with in the past? Have you hired new people? And if so, what are the attributes that make somebody new to you likely to be a fit and an affable?

Speaker 1 | 1:02:59 - 1:03:24
So it's a mixture. So, I mean, AlphaStar was an exceptional team. It was sort of intentionally assembled within DeepMind by choosing the kind of best of the best to work on that project. So in some sense, it's not a surprise that I think actually four of our co founders come from that team. But we are not exclusively drawing from that team or indeed from DeepMind.

Speaker 1 | 1:03:24 - 1:04:02
I mean, other three founders all came from very successful startups. And we hire people who are brilliant, but also kind and nice people to have around, who are gonna work together well, who are aligned with the mission and who, you know, fit the things that we that we need. So... But in terms of finding those people, we put a lot of effort into getting the right people. So as uncomfortable as it is, I've had to say no to a lot of people I've worked with in the past just because our bar is so super high.

Speaker 1 | 1:04:02 - 1:04:29
I've worked... I've been fortunate to work with, like, some amazing people. And so, you know, I've been choosing amongst, a very exceptional prop and bringing in what I consider to be a superstar team. And so, yeah, it's not easy to get into ineffable, but the people who we have are wonderful human beings and very, very proud of the people we've brought in.

Speaker 2 | 1:04:29 - 1:04:59
I can see why people are drawn to working in ineffable, especially the time when the biggest clusters, the biggest labs are kind of, they're locked in this prisoner's dilemma race. And there's a lot of dollars at stake. And the decisions get made differently. I can imagine for a set of people that especially really, really deeply believes in the scientific mission of what you want to accomplish, this must feel like a breath of fresh air.

Speaker 1 | 1:04:59 - 1:05:46
Yeah, I think that's right. And we've tried to establish a research led culture. So it's not a company that's led by building an incremental next product V17.1 on the thing that's come before. It's a company that's built on researchers pursuing their passion and trying to produce the breakthroughs that they believe are possible. And we center the company around that from the beginning and from the outset to create like a haven for research, you know, where we push back on product pressure because we believe that if we make these breakthroughs, it will lead to far bigger products downstream and far bigger successes than if we kind of start off from day one on, oh, here's the product we're doing from the beginning.

Speaker 1 | 1:05:47 - 1:05:57
So, yeah, so it's research led. We're creating, I think, a really special environment and, yeah, people are loving it. I'm loving it.

Speaker 2 | 1:05:57 - 1:06:23
Wonderful. Wonderful. I'd love to close with some predictions, maybe especially since you're such a super forecaster. What's your guess for when you'll have the first strong evidence that the approach is working? And then what's your forecast for when we'll achieve the mission that you've set out to achieve this first contact with superintelligence?

Speaker 1 | 1:06:24 - 1:06:30
Yeah. So these are fair questions. So there are gonna be some reasonable bars of uncertainty on this.

Speaker 2 | 1:06:30 - 1:06:32
Yeah. But you're being recorded, so we're gonna hold you to it.

Speaker 1 | 1:06:32 - 1:07:04
Exactly. Yeah. So I think we will see some extremely strong evidence that we're on the right track within a year. And I think we will achieve something which is a true super intelligence, according to the definition I gave earlier of something which discovers things which are far beyond what humans can achieve across everything from science, mathematics, technology, languages, etcetera, etcetera. I originally thought within three to five years, my timelines have accelerated a little bit.

Speaker 1 | 1:07:04 - 1:07:14
I'm gonna say three years because of, yeah, what can be done with with, like, coding agents to accelerate things. I think things are going to move fast.

Speaker 2 | 1:07:14 - 1:07:28
Buckle up. It's been a journey. Wonderful. Let's say, David, this is a wonderful, wonderful conversation. I'm so inspired by what you're building, and thank you for taking the time to sit down and share with our audience what you're building today.

Speaker 1 | 1:07:28 - 1:07:30
Thank you, Sanyat. Thank It's a pleasure.

items.title: Beam: The Great American Open Model with ReflectionAI Co-Founder and CEO Misha Laskin
items.author: No Priors
items.text:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:26
When you remove cyber offensive capabilities, you also remove cyber defensive capabilities. The state of the world today is that we have a few 100 safety researchers within closed labs that understand how these things work. And despite their best intentions, is impossible to cover the long tail of unintended consequences that these systems might have. A very powerful closed model went and hacked into another company, and the only way that company could remediate itself was by using open models to protect itself. That's the empirical evidence of the world that we're in.

Speaker 1 | 00:26 - 00:34
Linus' law, with enough eyeballs, all bugs become shallow. I have the belief that with enough eyeballs, most security and safety vulnerabilities become shallow as well.

Speaker 2 | 00:41 - 00:57
Today, we're joined by Misha Laskom, the co founder and CEO of Reflection AI. Reflection provides open weight models to power the future of intelligence. Misha Pryor was a researcher at Google DeepMind and received his PhD in Physics. Welcome, Inno Pryor's. Great to have you here today.

Speaker 1 | 00:57 - 00:59
Yeah, it's great to be here. Thanks for having me.

Speaker 2 | 00:59 - 01:11
Could you give us an update on where things are at? Mean, obviously, you guys have been pioneering really interesting work in open weights and open source models, particularly with a US bent. Can you talk a bit what you've been up to and what you guys have been building?

Speaker 1 | 01:11 - 01:38
Yeah, so for the last twelve months, we set, right, the mission of the company to build frontier open intelligence and make it widely accessible. And effectively, it's been a sprint to set up a lab that is capable of of doing such things. It it kind of feels like maybe there's a Reid Hoffman quote that, you know, you're assembling a a plane as you're flying it. And that's, you know, that... That's been the case.

Speaker 1 | 01:38 - 02:05
We were maybe around 30 people about a year ago, but it does take order of a 100 plus. So a couple 100 researchers and engineers to build one of these things, a true rocket ship project. And we're now at around 300 people and assembled all the teams on pre training, mid training, reinforcement learning, scaled up our... Trained our first models end to end and just released a model called Beam, which is Reflection's first open model.

Speaker 2 | 02:05 - 02:32
What has been the most challenging part of that? Because when people talk about scale or scaling up models or starting to build these models out, one issue is compute and procuring enough, a training cluster that's cohesive in terms of the ability to use it. Second is talent. And obviously, there's been these huge talent wars in terms of how much people pay for researchers, etcetera. Third is scale of data.

Speaker 2 | 02:33 - 02:35
Which of those has been the most limiting or the most challenging?

Speaker 1 | 02:35 - 02:50
What's been interesting about this experience is that I got asked this questions at all hands at the company, what's been the hardest thing last in year? And the reality is that everything is extremely hard. Everything has been hard.

Speaker 2 | 02:51 - 02:52
Startup, yeah.

Speaker 1 | 02:52 - 03:13
And it's also sometimes people might ask, well, what's the thing that really made your models work better than others or something like this? And again, the answer is everything. You actually have to get 30 things right, and that's why everything is hard because you have to get 30 things right. You have to get the talent. You have to retain the talent.

Speaker 1 | 03:13 - 03:31
You have to have a strong mission and culture that keeps the talent working together and rowing in the same boat. You have to get the data. You have to get the compute. You have to build the infrastructure to ensure that the compute is actually usable. These are...

Speaker 1 | 03:31 - 03:55
A lot of these things, when you're at an existing big lab, there have been years of build out that enabled them to have this kind of stable surface. So I was at DeepMind before this. A lot of the tools that we just take for granted, or I took for granted as a researcher because they just worked, You have to build. So I would say, yeah, everything has been hard, but also very rewarding that you can do it.

Speaker 3 | 03:55 - 04:04
Can you talk a little bit... You said about a year ago, you guys really committed to do this. Can you talk about the the sort of shift in ambition and commitment and what drove that?

Speaker 1 | 04:04 - 04:27
When we started the company about two and a half years ago, our bet was... So maybe I'll contextualize it, where the world was then. My cofounder, Janus, and I had been working on the first series of Gemini models. We were working on the reinforcement learning team. Janus was leading it, and we had just shipped the Gemini one and then 1.5 model.

Speaker 1 | 04:27 - 04:41
And that was... That early era, that was like similar to the first ChatGPT experience, which was primarily a chat experience. There was no coding really, nothing agentic. These models were just good at chat. And they were primarily...

Speaker 1 | 04:41 - 05:01
95% of the compute spent was spent on pre training. So they're primarily pre trained models. We are reinforcement learning researchers. That's been our lineage. Janus, my co founder, was one of the founding engineers at DeepMind and was a key contributor to all the big RL projects that came out of that lab, including AlphaGo.

Speaker 1 | 05:03 - 05:18
Our bet was because we were working on the RL team and we saw that RL for aligning chat models works. There's only so much you can align them. Well, now there's a lot more. Now they're agents. But at the time they were just chat.

Speaker 1 | 05:18 - 05:52
So RL was working and we just thought that, well, if you take that and apply it to domains where like mathematics, coding, that you could make these systems agentic. That was the big bet. And we thought that you could do this as an independent lab, much more capital efficiently because we started seeing open source, open models materialize. There was a small model from Mistral at the time. LAMA two had just released, and we saw LAMA three coming.

Speaker 3 | 05:53 - 05:55
We This feels like ages ago.

Speaker 1 | 05:55 - 06:21
Yeah. Yeah. This was a while back, I guess two years ago. And we thought that there'd be a great open model base that someone would build that we could build on and do our research and scale reinforcement learning. And over that first year of the company, ended up happening was that, one, reinforcement learning started working faster than we thought it would, both within our experiments, but also within industry.

Speaker 1 | 06:21 - 06:49
'one came out at that time. We actually thought it would take longer just because the journey from ImageNet in 2012 to RL systems that worked at scale was about four years. So we thought maybe something similar, but every year moves faster than my prediction, the previous year. And so about a year into the company, we got to the point where they're actually... All the good open models are coming from China.

Speaker 1 | 06:49 - 07:36
There were not really good Western open models. And we needed one as a base for the technology that we were building and decided for a number of reasons that the most impactful thing we could do, given the state of play, was to just build open models ourselves end to end, and combine the RL bet together with just building models end to end. I guess there were enterprise reasons, there were geopolitical reasons happening, but also there was the research reason that it turned out you actually do need to pre train your model in order to make reinforcement learning work very well at scale. So you actually kind of do need to do... The things are just so tightly coupled that you do need to do both.

Speaker 3 | 07:37 - 08:05
The conventional wisdom has been that pre training at the scale of the frontier is impossibly expensive or at least extraordinarily so. Clearly, there's been a huge shift of compute toward post training. Feel free not to answer this, and we can just cut it. But, like, what do you... How how did you think about just the resources needed or the ratio, or did you have, like, design principles, like, around the model that this feel tenable to you at the beginning, or you just say, we need to do this.

Speaker 3 | 08:05 - 08:06
We'll go resource it.

Speaker 1 | 08:06 - 08:35
Well, the the nice thing about being an open model lab is that you can also talk about things openly. Uh-huh. So you do need a lot of resources to to build something meaningful. You don't need the same amount of resources. Once you get to the frontier and you're really, really at the frontier of intelligence, then you need the same amount of resources as any other frontier lab, because you can kind of think about research as exploration of new ideas versus execution of known ideas.

Speaker 1 | 08:36 - 08:54
Part of why getting great talent matters a lot is because you get to cut down on exploration and focus on execution of the things that work. All this is to say is that if you are catching up to the frontier, you can do it a lot more capital efficiently.

Speaker 2 | 08:54 - 08:57
How much capital do you think it would take to catch up to the frontier?

Speaker 1 | 08:57 - 09:17
Well, I think that it depends on the frontier keeps moving. So each year it's actually more capital. And I'll get back to the question on the resourcing between, let's say, pre training and post training. I would say that a year ago, or maybe eighteen months ago, would have been... And I say orders, meaning that order of a 100,000,000, so hundreds of millions of

Speaker 2 | 09:17 - 09:18
dollars. I

Speaker 1 | 09:18 - 09:46
think that now, or let's say even six months ago, was probably order billion, so billions of dollars, single digit billions. Going into next year, I think order 10... Can kind of think about it as for every generation of model, there's a 4x multiplier in compute roughly. One heuristic that I have is when... Let's say we talk about the chips that are currently considered the ones that...

Speaker 1 | 09:46 - 10:09
A frontier chip and maybe a couple of years ago was an H100, and maybe it was a 100,000 H100s. Then Astra was trained, and that was just a big run on a 100,000 Blackwells, which is roughly a 4X multiplier on an H100. Now the next generation is gonna be around a 100,000 Vera Rubins, I believe. So that kind of gives you the scale. It moves from hundreds of millions to billions to tens of billions.

Speaker 2 | 10:09 - 10:28
Yeah. It seems like at some point that has to asymptote then because ultimately, relative to revenue scale of these companies, even potential revenue scale, you start to tap out in terms of the ability to invest against what you're actually gonna produce from an economic value perspective. Absolutely. So do you think we're heading into that asymptote in terms of model size or at least training cluster size?

Speaker 1 | 10:28 - 10:40
Absolutely. I think that in terms of... You know, there's only so much CapEx that you can do. Right? And Frontier Labs are now putting hundreds of billions of dollars into it.

Speaker 1 | 10:40 - 11:11
So will they be putting trillions of dollars in the next year or two? It's probably unlikely, but there are a couple of things that are happening. One is that the use of that compute is becoming a lot more efficient because the models are themselves becoming tools that help build themselves. So I think that when it was just human researchers doing the work, there's probably a 7X improvement each year. And you can actually track these things very technically.

Speaker 1 | 11:11 - 11:28
And in pre training, you do it by... You have your pre training loss, and then you measure your compute efficiency gains against... You made some changes. Now you have a new pre training loss, and it should be that you got to the same point with less compute. And so when you say 7x, it's actually a very concrete thing that you're studying.

Speaker 1 | 11:29 - 11:49
And now I would say across the systems of... I mean, pretraining is probably a bit more hardened, but there's a lot lot of of headroom in reinforcement learning. We're probably at a point where it's 30X like efficiency, depending how good your model is for actually improving itself. So that is one thing that's happening. 30X per year

Speaker 2 | 11:49 - 11:50
or over what?

Speaker 1 | 11:50 - 12:03
Yeah. Something like that. Yeah. I mean, it depends on what metric it is, but it roughly... I do think that the speed is probably four or more times faster than researchers just doing it alone, and they'll probably accelerate.

Speaker 1 | 12:03 - 12:44
So the amount of intelligence you can extract per training FLOP is is increasing. So at some point, that asymptote is okay. And then also, like, the amount of revenue that each FLOP can generate also increases, right, the more you pack intelligence. So going back to the question around how does this distribute across pretraining and reinforcement learning and to train beam, which is a 500,000,000,000 parameter model total 23 b active, it was 6,000 GB 300s. We ran it, I think, for a few weeks, but now with infrastructure efficiencies, we can do it in about twelve days, maybe less.

Speaker 1 | 12:45 - 13:10
There's a coupling of scientific and infrastructure efficiencies. Reinforcement learning was a little over 10,000 GB300s for four weeks. So actually there were more flops spent on reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning jobs are more complex in the sense that you do both a lot of inference at scale with all sorts of sandboxes for agents and training. This is actually...

Speaker 1 | 13:10 - 13:30
The reason I got into AI was I saw my co founder's work on AlphaGo, and I was a physicist at the time. There was a moment, there was a plot in AlphaGo where it just never stopped improving. It just kept improving. And they just cut it off at some point because what's the point of improving it further? You already beat the world champion.

Speaker 1 | 13:30 - 13:59
And I thought that, well, if you start to apply... Figure out how to apply that recipe to stuff that is economically valuable, then at that point it becomes an economic question of how much money do I want to put in to get to just keep improving the system. And we, a field, are there. And one of the things that I'm really excited about in this open source project and the tech report that we'll have in it is that we'll describe how these things are built. And indeed, this reinforcement learning system never stopped learning.

Speaker 1 | 13:59 - 14:26
If you look at our plots, they just keep going up. And it's just a matter of compute basically in terms of scaling it further. That is to say, we as a field are there where you have these RL systems that are very general that don't really stop improving. You want to make them a lot more efficient to extract the most intelligence from your compute. But that means that you move from a question of, you train these things to where can you get the data and what is economically valuable?

Speaker 1 | 14:26 - 14:39
And it's just an economics decision of how much money do I put into X to get some kind of improvement out of it, which is incredible. That's a... Yeah. Yeah. This was not true two years ago.

Speaker 3 | 14:39 - 14:45
What can you share about where you've already decided we should turn the crank in terms of just continuing to invest in capability?

Speaker 1 | 14:45 - 15:11
This is almost to some kind of dissatisfaction to some scientists and that it's moved... I mean, it is a science, but it's... I would say feels more of an engineering discipline. It seems more like, again, the rocket ship analogy and the way that building rockets is a science, but most people think about it as an engineering discipline with some scientific work in it. And that's roughly how it feels.

Speaker 1 | 15:11 - 15:29
So I... The stages are kind of set and that they're... The axes of scaling are today. And now there might be something kind of totally blue ocean that we don't know, and there's some new labs exploring it. But it's pre training, synthetic data, reinforcement learning.

Speaker 1 | 15:29 - 15:53
Or in some sense you can say just training and reinforcement learning. And there are architectural improvements that can be made. There are data improvements, algorithmic improvements, but it doesn't feel like a wild west the way I felt five years ago or something. Like the... Something that was kind of beautiful about both think DeepMind and Google Brain.

Speaker 1 | 15:53 - 16:23
And even if you look at early OpenAI is how diverse the bets were, and people were doing just crazy fun stuff. And now it's really narrowed in. And part of it, there's also a bit of a hardware lottery kind of thing, because once something starts working, the hardware also starts co optimizing against it, and so it's harder to find... Even if you have a great new idea, if it's not really a good fit for the hardware, it doesn't make sense. So to answer your question, I don't see...
